1: Welcome back to Building Global Secure Access.
This is Chapter 6: private applications and administrative paths.
A VPN gives a device an address range.
Private Access gives a group one application, on its ports, behind its own Conditional Access.
The code checks that each app is that narrow, and that administrative paths ask for phishing-resistant authentication.
The chapter is a draft awaiting review, and the code is illustrative, tested against fixtures.
2: Because a compromised user or device on a VPN address pool can move laterally across everything the pool reaches.
Private Access replaces the range with one application for one group, behind that application's own policy.

So the goal: show, application by application, that each reaches only its host and ports, only for its group, under a policy that excludes emergency access; that administrative RDP and SSH require phishing-resistant authentication; and that connectors survive a patch night.
It's for the developers, the server and application owners, and the privileged access owner.
3: Learn's Private Access tutorial creates an application from the custom template, marks it a Private Access app, binds it to a connector group, adds its segments and assigns a group with the app's user role.
Segments may not overlap between per-app applications; a per-app segment overrides Quick Access; and clients can take fifteen minutes to see a change.
Connectors are read with a write-capable permission and report active or inactive, and their version.
Learn's Zero Trust recommendations ask for two healthy, current connectors per group, least-privilege segments and every app assigned.
And for domain controllers, the sensor starts in audit, with application service names before the DC's own.
4: What does it leave to you?
The requests create one app, but nothing reads all of them back with their segments and assignments, so the kit has a read for that, marked unverified, and the lab compares it with the portal.
A group with one inactive connector looks fine in a list, so the kit counts active members.
A wide range on every port is the VPN again, so wide segments and overlaps fail.
A person assigned directly escapes the access review.
Plain M F A on RDP passes a casual look, so any app covering port 22 or 3389 needs the phishing-resistant strength and a compliant device.
And Quick Access is tracked until it's empty.
5: Two or more active connectors per group, each at the minimum version.
Segments left in Quick Access, a warning until there are none.
Each segment a host or a narrow range, on named ports, with no overlaps.
A policy that targets the app and excludes the emergency group.
RDP and SSH apps that require the phishing-resistant strength and a compliant device.
And the last day's private sessions by destination, to compare with the assignments.
The administrative policy is a reviewed file, the guide's own; when the tenant's copy drifts, the plan brings it back.
6: Application owners own their app's assignment and review it each quarter.
The platform owner for servers keeps two healthy, current connectors in every group.
The privileged access owner owns the administrative apps and the domain controller sensor, and that's where Building Privileged Access comes in, for the privileged groups behind them.

For permissions: a write-capable delegated permission for the connector reads, an application read for the apps, which isn't verified yet, the policy permissions, and three administrator roles activated just for the lab.

10: Lab 2 needs a test tenant with Private Access licenses, a connector group with two connectors on Windows Server 2019 or later, a test server and a pilot group.
Publish one app with the guide's own requests, named so the kit's reviewed policy file finds it, one host on 443, for the pilot group.
Collect and check, comparing the app read with the portal first; the policy check fails, because there's no policy yet.
Plan and apply its policy in report-only.
Then validate: from a device off the corporate network, the host is reachable on 443 and not on another port.
Back it out by deleting the policy, then the application.
The authors haven't run this lab.
11: Narrow apps for one group support access enforcement, least privilege and managed access control points.

Phishing-resistant administrative paths support multifactor authentication and logging privileged functions; the guide lists O M B M twenty-two oh-nine's phishing-resistant M F A and VPN-free application access among the requirements this supports.

The dangers: a wide segment, a group with one connector, plain M F A on RDP, Quick Access left as a range, and protecting a domain controller's own service name before the applications', which can lock administrators out.
You're done when every group, every app and every administrative path passes.
